title: Hawks' Jalen Johnson Must Improve His Shooting
text:
Hawks' Jalen Johnson Must Improve His Shooting

 Dale Zanine-Imagn Images Dale Zanine-Imagn Images Hawks Need More From Jalen Johnson as Shooting Struggles Mount
 JamesPiercey Partner Nov 11, 2026 4:58 PM Published Nov 11, 2026 4:58 PM Updated Nov 17, 2026 5:20 PM Jalen Johnson is still filling the box score, but his efficiency has slipped. The Hawks need more from their franchise player.
 More Videos The Atlanta Hawks ' franchise player is Jalen Johnson. If they're going to have a successful 2026-27 NBA season, they're going to need more from him.
 Johnson isn't entirely to blame for the Hawks' shortcomings so far. Still, he'll get the lion's share of the blame. That's what happens when you're a franchise player.
 And there's no shortage of legitimate criticisms of Johnson's play so far this year.
 Hawks' Johnson Must Be More Efficient
 Johnson has been productive. The counting stats are still there. Through nine games, he's averaging 19.2 points, 8.6 rebounds, and 7.2 assists per contest, after missing three games with a left ankle sprain .
 Related stories
 The biggest issues are with his efficiency. Johnson is shooting 44.9% from the field and an ugly 20.5% from deep, including 6-of-14 and 0-of-3 in Monday's 124-114 loss to the Los Angeles Lakers. That makes for a below-average 54.1% True Shooting Percentage (TS%).
 It seems to be affecting his overall impact on the game. Last season, Johnson had an impressive 4.2 Box Plus/Minus (BPM), and he's down to 1.1 in 2026-27.
 There's always some noise in those stats. Plus/minus numbers are reflective of the team's performance above all else. Still, it feels fair to say that the Hawks ought to be better when Johnson is on the floor.
 So what gives?
 Hawks' Johnson Must Adjust His Approach
 On some level, there are roster construction issues here. Johnson often shares the floor with fellow non-shooter Dyson Daniels, which can make the Hawks easier to guard. That shouldn't be taken as proof of Johnson's deficiencies, but it is concerning.
 Simply speaking, Johnson is struggling to score in the half-court. Defenses are collapsing on him in the paint. When he does get there, he scores efficiently , but his inability to score from any other area makes him too easy to guard.
 It's an issue many point-forward types have historically had. Defenses used to collapse on LeBron James until he learned how to make them pay with improved shooting.
 Johnson needs to take a page specifically from his book.
 It's a big ask. Nobody is saying Johnson needs to become a sniper overnight, but adding a more reliable mid-range shot could do wonders for his game.
 That said, the mid-range wasn't a big part of Johnson's game last year, and he thrived. It's difficult to diagnose what's different this year, but something clearly has to give. The Hawks have pinned their hopes on Johnson.
 So, they need him to be better.
